name: Ancient History – Buddhism: Life of Buddha, Teachings, Organization & Sects

notes.heading: Overview
points: Buddhism was founded by Gautama Buddha in the 6th century BCE
It emerged as a reform movement against ritualistic Vedic practices
Focuses on ethical living, non-violence, and liberation from suffering
Spread widely across India and Asia through missionary efforts

notes.heading: Birth and Life of Buddha (563–483 BCE)
points: Born as Siddhartha Gautama in Lumbini (modern Nepal)
Belonged to Shakya clan of Kshatriyas
Father: Suddhodana (ruler of Kapilavastu)
Mother: Queen Maya (Mahamaya)
Wife: Yashodhara; son: Rahula

notes.heading: Four Sights and Renunciation
points: Saw an old man, sick man, dead body, and ascetic
Realized suffering is universal
Left palace at age of 29 (Mahabhinishkramana)
Practiced severe austerity and meditation
Attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya under Bodhi tree

notes.heading: Enlightenment and Death
points: Attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya (Bihar)
Became Buddha (the Enlightened One)
Delivered first sermon at Sarnath (Dharmachakra Pravartana)
Died at Kushinagar at age of 80 (Mahaparinirvana)
Final words emphasized self-reliance and diligence

notes.heading: Teachings of Buddha – Core Philosophy
points: Four Noble Truths (Arya Satya)
Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga)
Middle Path (avoid extremes of luxury and austerity)
Emphasis on morality, meditation, and wisdom
Rejection of caste system and ritual sacrifices

notes.heading: Four Noble Truths
points: Life is suffering (Dukkha)
Cause of suffering is desire (Trishna)
Suffering can be ended (Nirvana)
Path to end suffering is Eightfold Path

notes.heading: Eightfold Path
points: Right Understanding
Right Thought
Right Speech
Right Action
Right Livelihood
Right Effort
Right Mindfulness
Right Concentration

notes.heading: Other Teachings
points: Doctrine of impermanence (Anicca)
No permanent soul (Anatta)
Karma and rebirth concept
Non-violence (Ahimsa)
Ethical and moral discipline

notes.heading: Organization of Buddhism – Sangha
points: Monastic order of monks and nuns
Founded by Buddha at Sarnath
Open to all castes and classes
Based on discipline (Vinaya rules)
Supported spread of Buddhism

notes.heading: Features of Sangha
points: Democratic functioning with assemblies
Strict code of conduct (Vinaya Pitaka)
Bhikshus (monks) and Bhikshunis (nuns)
Dependent on alms for survival
Played key role in missionary expansion

notes.heading: Buddhist Councils
points: First Council: Rajagriha – compiled teachings
Second Council: Vaishali – early sect division
Third Council: Pataliputra – under Ashoka
Fourth Council: Kashmir – under Kanishka
Helped in codification and spread of Buddhism

notes.heading: Sects of Buddhism
points: Hinayana (Theravada) – strict original teachings
Mahayana – liberal, worship of Buddha as god-like
Vajrayana – tantric practices, later development
Hinayana focuses on individual liberation
Mahayana emphasizes Bodhisattva ideal

notes.heading: Differences between Hinayana and Mahayana
points: Hinayana: Buddha as teacher; Mahayana: Buddha as divine
Hinayana: individual salvation; Mahayana: universal salvation
Hinayana: Pali language; Mahayana: Sanskrit texts
Hinayana: conservative; Mahayana: flexible
Hinayana: Theravada dominant in Sri Lanka and SE Asia

notes.heading: Importance of Buddhism
points: Social reform movement against caste system
Promoted non-violence and ethical living
Encouraged education and literacy
Spread across Asia (Sri Lanka, China, Japan)
Influenced Indian art, architecture, and culture

name: Ancient History – Buddhism: Literature, Councils, Spread, Royal Patronage & Decline

notes.heading: Overview
points: Buddhism developed a rich literary tradition and organized doctrinal texts
Buddhist councils played key role in codifying teachings
Royal patronage (especially Ashoka and Kanishka) helped its spread
Buddhism spread across Asia through missionaries and trade routes
Gradual decline occurred in India due to multiple religious and social factors

notes.heading: Literature of Buddhism – General Features
points: Buddhist literature written in Pali and Sanskrit
Deals with philosophy, discipline, and teachings of Buddha
Preserved orally before being written down
Divided into Tripitaka (Three Baskets)
Important source for early Indian history

notes.heading: Tripitaka – Buddhist Canon
points: Vinaya Pitaka – rules for monks and nuns
Sutta Pitaka – sermons and teachings of Buddha
Abhidhamma Pitaka – philosophical analysis
Forms core of Theravada Buddhist texts
Represents earliest Buddhist doctrinal compilation

notes.heading: Other Important Buddhist Texts
points: Jataka Tales – stories of Buddha’s previous lives
Buddhacarita – life of Buddha by Ashvaghosha
Milindapanha – dialogue between King Menander and monk Nagasena
Lalitavistara – life of Buddha (Mahayana tradition)
Divyavadana – collection of Buddhist legends

notes.heading: Buddhist Councils
points: First Council – Rajagriha: compiled Buddha’s teachings after his death
Second Council – Vaishali: led to early schism in Sangha
Third Council – Pataliputra (under Ashoka): purification of Sangha
Fourth Council – Kashmir (under Kanishka): compilation of Mahayana texts
Helped in doctrinal consolidation and sect formation

notes.heading: Significance of Councils
points: Preservation of teachings
Resolution of doctrinal disputes
Development of sects (Hinayana and Mahayana)
Standardization of Buddhist canon
Strengthened institutional structure of Buddhism

notes.heading: Spread of Buddhism
points: Spread within India during Mauryan period
Ashoka sent missionaries to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, West Asia
Spread through trade routes like Silk Route
Monasteries acted as centers of learning
Adopted by foreign rulers and communities

notes.heading: Role of Royal Patronage
points: Ashoka – greatest patron; promoted Dhamma and sent missionaries
Kanishka – patron of Mahayana Buddhism
Indo-Greek rulers supported Buddhism (e.g., Menander)
Gupta rulers were more inclined towards Hinduism but tolerated Buddhism
Royal support helped construction of stupas and monasteries

notes.heading: Major Centres of Buddhism
points: Magadha (Bihar) – early center
Sarnath – first sermon
Nalanda – major learning university
Taxila – center of learning
Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia – major Theravada centers

notes.heading: Causes for the Decline of Buddhism in India
points: Rise of Brahmanical Hinduism and Bhakti movement
Loss of royal patronage after Mauryas and Guptas
Corruption and degeneration in monastic order
Complexity of Mahayana rituals alienated common people
Invasions (Hunas, later Turkic invasions) destroyed monasteries

notes.heading: Social and Religious Causes of Decline
points: Absorption of Buddha as avatar of Vishnu in Hinduism
Decline of simple teachings of Buddha
Language barrier (shift from Pali to Sanskritized texts)
Rigid monastic life disconnected from society
Competition from Jainism and Hinduism

notes.heading: Institutional Causes of Decline
points: Dependence on royal patronage
Wealth accumulation in monasteries
Loss of missionary zeal
Fragmentation into sects
Decline of educational institutions after invasions

notes.heading: Significance of Buddhism Despite Decline
points: Lasting impact on Indian art and architecture
Influence on Hindu philosophy (Ahimsa, Karma)
Spread across Asia (Sri Lanka, China, Japan, Tibet)
Development of universities like Nalanda
Cultural and ethical legacy in Indian society
